chapters.title: A Letter That Changed Its Mind
chapters.teaser: Jude says he had to abandon a warmer letter to write this urgent one instead.
body: Jude admits he meant to write a different letter altogether — something about the salvation all believers share, presumably encouraging — but circumstances pushed him toward something sharper: an urgent call to "earnestly contend for the faith" (v.3).

That faith, he says, was "once delivered unto the saints" — a fixed inheritance handed down, not something each generation gets to reinvent. The phrase sets the stakes for the whole letter: this isn't a polite difference of opinion, but a settled deposit under active attack from people who had quietly slipped in among the community (v.4).

chapters.title: Three Warnings from Israel's Past
chapters.teaser: Jude reaches for three ancient precedents to show that privilege doesn't prevent judgment.
body: Jude lines up three precedents from Israel's past in quick succession: the generation God rescued from Egypt but later destroyed for unbelief (v.5), angels who abandoned their proper place and are now held in chains of darkness (v.6), and Sodom and Gomorrah, left as a public example under eternal fire (v.7).

What ties all three together is that each group started out with real standing — rescued Israelites, heavenly angels, cities under God's own provision — and still came under judgment through rebellion. Jude's point is that being inside the community, even inside heaven itself, has never guaranteed protection from the consequences of abandoning one's calling.

chapters.title: Even an Archangel Held His Tongue
chapters.teaser: Michael's restraint toward the devil exposes just how reckless the false teachers really are.
body: Jude reaches for a striking, non-biblical tradition (echoing the Jewish text known as the Assumption of Moses) to make his point: even the archangel Michael, disputing with the devil over the body of Moses, didn't dare throw a slanderous accusation at him — he simply said, "The Lord rebuke thee" (v.9).

That restraint becomes the standard the false teachers fail: they slander things they don't even understand (v.10), indulging their appetites like unreasoning animals. If an archangel wouldn't presume to condemn Satan in his own words, Jude implies, these teachers have badly overstepped what's theirs to judge.

chapters.title: Waterless Clouds and Wandering Stars
chapters.teaser: Jude piles up nature images to expose false teachers as all promise and no substance.
body: Verses 12-13 read almost like a list of accusations in verse form: hidden reefs at the community's shared meals, clouds that promise rain and carry none, trees that should bear fruit but are doubly dead and uprooted, wild sea-waves foaming up their own shame, wandering stars kept for everlasting darkness.

Each picture attacks the same failure from a different angle — the appearance of substance with nothing real behind it. These are people who look impressive and confident at the community's own table, but produce nothing of value, and the very images meant to suggest stability end up exposing how unstable they actually are.

chapters.title: Enoch's Prophecy and a Doxology
chapters.teaser: Jude quotes a text outside the Bible, then ends with one of Scripture's most quoted blessings.
body: Jude quotes directly from 1 Enoch, a Jewish apocalyptic text outside the Hebrew Bible, crediting "Enoch, the seventh from Adam," with a prophecy of the Lord returning with countless holy ones to execute judgment on all (v.14-15) — a rare case of a New Testament writer openly citing something beyond the Old Testament canon.

Having spent most of the letter warning, Jude pivots at the end to instruction and hope: build yourselves up in the faith, pray in the Spirit, stay in God's love, show mercy to the wavering, and pull others out of the fire before it's too late (v.20-23). The closing doxology — praise to the God able to keep believers from falling and present them faultless with great joy (v.24) — outlasts every warning that came before it.
